summary: While Jesus teaches good news in the temple, chief priests, scribes, and elders challenge his authority. He answers with John's baptism, exposing their public calculation, then tells of tenants who beat servants, kill the beloved son, and lose stewardship; Psalm 118's rejected stone becomes cornerstone and threat. Spies ask whether paying tribute to Caesar is lawful. Jesus makes them identify the emperor's image on a denarius and demands what belongs to Caesar — and what belongs to God. Sadducees pose a seven-husband resurrection puzzle from levirate marriage. Jesus says resurrection life cannot be reduced to present household structures and argues from Moses's burning bush that God is God of the living. He then asks how David's son is also David's Lord and publicly warns against scribes who consume widows' houses while displaying devotion.
whyItMatters: Every trap in the chapter concerns authority: prophetic, economic, scriptural, familial, messianic, and institutional. Jesus neither evades the public world nor lets its categories become ultimate. Stewardship is accountable, empire cannot own God's image-bearers, resurrection transforms present arrangements, and religious display is judged by its treatment of widows.

context.author: Luke narrating Jerusalem temple disputes shared with the Synoptic tradition
context.audience: Communities under empire and in debate over authority, resurrection, Scripture, and leadership
context.setting: Temple courts in Jerusalem during Jesus's final teaching days
context.literaryForm: Challenge-riposte controversies, violent tenant parable, coin demonstration, resurrection debate, scriptural riddle, and public warning

outline.heading: Authority challenged and John's baptism returned as a question
Tenants, beloved son, rejected stone, and threatened stewards
Sadducees, seven husbands, and resurrection life

keyVerses.text: But he looked at them and said, “Then what is this that is written, ‘The stone which the builders rejected was made the chief cornerstone’?
keyVerses.why: Rejection becomes God's reversal while remaining a warning to leaders who misuse entrusted building work.

keyVerses.text: He said to them, “Then give to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.”
keyVerses.why: The answer acknowledges a limited civic claim while opening the unlimited question of what bears God's ownership.

keyVerses.text: Now he is not the God of the dead, but of the living, for all are alive to him.”
keyVerses.why: Jesus grounds resurrection hope in God's continuing covenant relation, not only in speculative mechanics.

questions.question: Why won't Jesus directly name his authority source?
questions.answer: The leaders' question is legitimate in principle, but their response to John's authority reveals calculated refusal: they fear the crowd and will not state what they believe. Jesus's counterquestion links his work to John's prophetic baptism and refuses to hand a slogan to people avoiding honest evaluation.

questions.question: Who are the tenants, and does the parable say God rejects Israel?
questions.answer: The vineyard evokes Israel, while tenants represent leaders entrusted with it, not the vineyard itself. Servants recall prophets; the beloved son intensifies accountability. Stewardship changes because of violent leadership. Turning that judgment into ‘church replaces Jews’ confuses people with managers and fuels anti-Judaism.

questions.question: Does ‘give to Caesar’ command unquestioning payment and obedience?
questions.answer: Jesus asks whose image and inscription the coin bears, then returns it to Caesar's sphere while demanding God's due. The answer escapes both collaboration and revolt traps but does not define Caesar's claim as unlimited. Humans bear God's image, so imperial ownership is relativized rather than sacralized.

questions.question: What was a denarius saying through its image and inscription?
questions.answer: Roman silver coins carried the emperor's portrait and titles that advertised imperial authority and sometimes divine associations. Using such a coin made the political-theological issue visible in Jesus's hand. His hearers produce the evidence of the system whose trap they pose.

questions.question: Who were the Sadducees?
questions.answer: They were a Jewish elite group associated especially with priestly and temple leadership, and Luke notes their denial of resurrection. They differed from Pharisees and should not be blended into one opponent class. Their puzzle uses Torah's levirate marriage duty to make resurrection look absurd.

questions.question: Does Jesus say people become angels?
questions.answer: He says resurrection people cannot die and are ‘like angels’ or equal to angels in that respect, not that humans change species. Marriage's present household and inheritance functions no longer organize life the same way. The text does not erase embodied identity; Luke 24 will stress Jesus's risen body.

questions.question: How does the burning bush prove resurrection?
questions.answer: Jesus cites God's self-identification as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, long after their deaths. Covenant relation is living and cannot end in annihilation; ‘all live to him.’ The argument is relational and grammatical, not a detailed timetable of intermediate state and bodily resurrection.

questions.question: Why end with scribes devouring widows' houses?
questions.answer: Long robes, greetings, chief seats, and long prayers create public piety, while exploitation destroys vulnerable households. Luke puts social consequence beside religious performance. The warning targets leaders who convert spiritual trust into economic access; it is not a rejection of scribal learning itself.

glossary.def: Cultivator working an owner's vineyard and owing its produce or rent.

Torah practice in which a brother married a childless widow to continue the deceased brother's line.
Jewish group linked to temple leadership and known here for denying resurrection.
